feedback: If a learner labels remora–shark as mutualism, prompt: apply the benefit test to the SECOND partner — does the shark actually gain anything? If it is unaffected, it is commensalism.

If a learner calls the tick a predator or a lion-eating-zebra parasitism, contrast the two: a predator kills and eats quickly; a parasite lives on or in a host over time, usually without killing it outright.
If a learner excludes the tick as 'not really symbiosis', restate that symbiosis is any close, long-term relationship between different species and parasitism is one of its kinds.

If a learner says the clownfish and anemone 'agree' to help each other, explain the benefit as an evolved relationship, not a conscious deal — each partner simply does what helps itself and both happen to gain.
On a borderline case, affirm that choosing 'not enough evidence' is good scientific caution: commensalism is often the hardest to verify because the 'unaffected' partner may be slightly affected.
activities.intendedInsight: The three vocabulary words become a reusable reasoning tool: any close, ongoing relationship between different species can be classified by tracking each partner's cost or benefit, so a harmful case (parasitism) still counts as symbiosis.
learnerActions: For each presented pair — clownfish and anemone, remora and shark, tick and deer, a bird nesting in a tree — mark the outcome for EACH partner as benefit (+), no clear effect (0), or harm (–).
Read off the resulting type from the two marks: +/+ = mutualism, +/0 = commensalism, +/– = parasitism.
Meet a brand-new pair (e.g. barnacles on a whale) you were not taught and classify it yourself by asking 'does the whale lose anything?'
When a card shows predation (a lion eating a zebra) or competition between members of the same species, reject it as NOT symbiosis and say why.
On deliberately fuzzy cases, choose a 'not enough evidence' response if the second partner's gain or loss is genuinely hard to tell.
activities.title: Classify the relationship from outcomes

feedback: For a mislabelled sort, ask the learner to state each partner's + / 0 / – before re-sorting.
For a rejected-distractor miss, restate that symbiosis is a close, ongoing relationship, unlike a brief lethal predatory act.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can distinguish the three types and holds the boundary that predation and competition are not symbiosis.
learnerActions: Sort a set of pairs into mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
Answer a multiple-choice item classifying a new scenario and justify the choice.
Reject distractor cards showing predation or same-species competition as not-symbiosis.
activities.title: Sort and classify check
